newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - May 22.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - May 22.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

Following an announcement by Immigration Minister Philip Ruddock that immigration would be cut by 6,000 in 1997/98, business groups say the decision is politically motivated and does not meet the needs of the economy. Ruddock insisted the cut was due to high levels of unemployment and not in response to the rising popularity of Pauline Hanson. Page 1.

The Federal Government's Information Policy Advisory Council chairman Dr Terry Cutler, a key adviser to Communications Minister Richard Alston, said Australia should look at relaxing foreign investment rules to ensure the development of an online industry. Cutler, along with senior media executives, said the issue was vital to the future economic development of Australia. Page 3.

Federal Treasurer Peter Costello said yesterday the Government would not move to reform Australia's current tax system in this term of office, but promised any proposed reforms would be released before the next election. Costello also ruled out a national summit on tax reform, claiming the Labor summit held in 1985 was not successful. Page 3.

Prime Minister John Howard told a business function in Sydney yesterday his Government is confident economic growth will reach four percent by the end of 1997, even though current activity remains uneven. Howard said that by world economic standards, Australia has a very high level of economic growth. Page 5.
THE AUSTRALIAN

The Federal Government has made further immigration cuts, nearly halving the family reunion programme, but increasing the number of skilled migrants. Immigration Minister Philip Ruddock said yesterday high levels of unemployment had led to the decision, yet the move was condemned by ethnic community leaders. Page 1.

Police said yesterday they hold grave fears for Kerry Whelan, a mother of three and wife of a millionaire Sydney businessman, who was kidnapped in western Sydney on May 6. Her abductors are demanding A$1 million in ransom, but failed to make contact with husband Bernard Whelan by last Friday. Page 1.

The Federal Government granted a visa to Taiwanese Minister of State Yang Shih-chin, who was refused a visa in November last year at a time of hostility with China. News of the visit by Yang's delegation three weeks ago, kept low key to ensure no irritaton to China, comes on the eve of a visit by China's Vice-Premier Zhu Rongji. Page 1.

Following the Federal Government's rejection of a Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission finding that the removal of 100,000 Aboriginal children from their families was an act of genocide, Independent MP Pauline Hanson claimed the policy of assimilation adopted between 1910 and 1970 has allowed many Aborigines to still be alive today. Page 3.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

In move which will see the Federal Government again go head to head with the Senate, the Coalition is planning legislation to give it more power to control immigration, as Immigration Minister Philip Ruddock yesterday announced Cabinet had approved a cut of 6,000 in immigration. Page 1.

In his first public response to the report on the separation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children from their parents, Federal Attorney-General Daryl Williams said last night there would be no payment of compensation to Aboriginal children who were systematically seized from their parents from the beginning of the European colonisation up to the 1970s. Williams claimed payouts would be "inappropriate and divisive". Page 1.

Senior academic Professor Lauchlan Chipman, a member of the Howard Government's inquiry into higher education, said overseas students studying in Australia are being offered up to A$500 to switch universities. Chipman believes the poaching places Australia's A$3 billion a year international education market at risk. Page 1.

Police yesterday lifted a six-day media ban, revealing details of the kidnapping of Kerry Whelan, the wife of Sydney company director Bernard Whelan. Mrs Whelan was last known to be seen leaving her keys with an attendant at the underground carpark of the Parramatta Park Royal on May 6, and police said she was kidnapped for ransom. Page 1.
THE AGE

Under radical road laws proposed by the Victorian Government, police would have to power to demand blood and urine samples from drivers they believe may be under the influence of drugs. The proposal was immediately criticised by the Australian Medical Asociation, and Liberty Victoria. Page 1.

Victorian Premier Jeff Kennett yesterday resisted calls for the sacking of his former Health Minister Marie Tehan, after Tehan admitted that she was unable to explain how she failed to see a sensitive memo on the Intergraph affair. While Kennett defended Tehan, he did leave the way open for action against her, challenging the Opposition to produce more evidence. Page 1.

In a move it claims is a response to high unemployment, and not to the calls of Pauline Hanson, the Federal Government has announced a cut in migrant intake of 6,000 for the next financial year. The intake of 12,000 under the humanitarian programme will remain unchanged. Page 1.

The Private Health Insurance Administration Council yesterday released figures showing Australians are continuing to drop private health cover despite tax incentives from the Federal Government. The Council said there was a 0.7 percent fall in numbers, which equates to 100,000 people dropping their insurance. Page 1.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
